prompt: In Go, what decides whether a value lives on the stack or on the heap?
hint: Section 02 asked something with `-gcflags=-m`.

choices.text: You do: `&` and `new` put a value on the heap, plain variables go on the stack
choices.why: That is C's rule. In Go `p := point{1, 2}` was a plain variable and still went to the heap, because its address left the function.

choices.text: The compiler, by escape analysis
choices.why: Right. It keeps a value in the frame when it can prove nothing uses it after the return, and moves it to the heap otherwise.

choices.text: The garbage collector
choices.why: The collector only frees heap values. Where a value goes was settled at compile time, and `-m` printed it without running anything.

choices.text: The operating system, which hands out the stack
choices.why: The kernel gives the process memory, but which variable goes where is the Go compiler's choice, made per value.

prompt: `newPoint` declares `p := point{1, 2}` and returns `&p`. What happens to `p`?
hint: Read the first line `-m` printed.

choices.text: It dies with the frame, and the caller is left holding a dangling pointer
choices.why: That is the C bug the section opened with. Go's compiler sees the address leave and does not let `p` die with the frame.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to return the address of a local
choices.why: It compiled and ran; `newPoint` allocated once per call in `AllocsPerRun`.

choices.text: It is copied into the caller's frame when the function returns
choices.why: The caller receives a pointer, so there is nothing to copy into; the value has to outlive the call somewhere else.

choices.text: It is moved to the heap, and the pointer the caller holds stays good
choices.why: Right: `moved to heap: p`. That is why lesson 23 could call returning it safe.

prompt: `count` and `squares` both call `make`. Why does only the array in `squares` escape?
hint: Look at what each function returns.

choices.text: `make` allocates on the heap by default, and the call in `count` was dropped as useless
choices.why: The call was kept: `-m` printed `make([]int, 0, 8) does not escape` about it, so the array was made, in the frame.

choices.text: `squares` returns the slice, so its array must outlive the call
choices.why: Right. `count` returns only a length, so nothing leads back to its array after the return.

choices.text: `squares` writes into its slice in a loop
choices.why: Writing into a slice says nothing about who can reach it later; `count` writes into its own with `append`.

choices.text: `append` in `count` moves the array to the stack
choices.why: `append` moves nothing to the stack. The array was in the frame from the `make` on, because it never escaped.

prompt: Which of these went to the heap in `~/memory`? Choose all that apply.
hint: `AllocsPerRun` counted one allocation for three of the five functions.

choices.text: `p` in `newPoint`
choices.why: Yes: its address is returned.

choices.text: `nums` in `sum`
choices.why: No. The array is only read inside the function, and `-m` printed nothing about it.

choices.text: `table` in `large`
choices.why: Yes, though nothing escapes: 1.6 MB is over the 128 KiB a declared variable may take in a frame.

choices.text: The array behind `buf` in `count`
choices.why: No: `does not escape`, and `count` allocated 0 times per call.

prompt: `go build -gcflags=___` makes the compiler print its decisions, including what escapes to the heap.
hint: One letter after a dash.

prompt: A function declares `var buf [1 << 20]byte`, a 1 MiB array, uses it and returns an `int`. Nothing takes its address. What does `-gcflags=-m` say about `buf`?
hint: Escape analysis is not the only rule that sends a value to the heap.

choices.text: Nothing: a value that does not escape always stays in the frame, whatever its size may be
choices.why: That holds below a size limit. `large` in `~/memory` escaped nothing and still got `moved to heap: table`.

choices.text: A compile error: the array is too large for a stack
choices.why: Go does not refuse it. A variable too big for the frame is put somewhere else, not rejected.

choices.text: `moved to heap: buf`, as 1 MiB is over the 128 KiB limit for a declared variable
choices.why: Right. `MaxStackVarSize` is 128 KiB, and the same thing happened to the 1.6 MB `table`.

choices.text: Nothing at compile time; the program overflows its stack when it runs
choices.why: The compiler acts first and moves it. A Go stack is not what a 1 MiB local array is put on.

prompt: Which heap values does Go's garbage collector free?
hint: It starts from the roots.

choices.text: Those unused for a while
choices.why: The collector never asks when a value was last used, nor how old it is; it is non-generational.

choices.text: The ones no pointer from a root leads to
choices.why: Right. Marking follows pointers from package variables and goroutine stacks; whatever it never reached is swept.

choices.text: The ones created by functions that have already returned
choices.why: `newPoint` returned and its `p` was kept, because the caller still pointed at it.

choices.text: The largest ones, once the heap passes the GOGC goal
choices.why: The goal decides when a collection starts, never which values go. A large reachable value is kept, as the 64 MB array was.

prompt: Match each field of `gc 3 @0.009s 2%: … 15->15->8 MB, 16 MB goal, … 4 P` to what it means.
hint: `go doc runtime` printed the key.

pairs.right: the third collection of the run
heap at the start, at the end, and still reachable
the size the collection aimed to finish under

right_distractors: how long the program was paused

prompt: A collection ends with 10 MB still reachable, and the program runs with `GOGC=200`. At what heap size, in MB, is the next collection's goal?
hint: `GOGC=100` let 8 MB grow to a 16 MB goal.

prompt: `gc 3` printed `0.027+0.29+0.058 ms clock`. For how long was the program stopped?
hint: Two of the three phases stop the world.

choices.text: 0.375 ms, all three phases added together
choices.why: The middle phase, marking, runs while the program does; adding it counts time the program was running.

choices.text: 0.29 ms, the longest phase
choices.why: That one is the concurrent mark, the part that does not stop anything.

choices.text: 0.085 ms, the first and the last phase
choices.why: Right: sweep termination and mark termination stop the world; the 0.29 ms between them ran beside the program.

choices.text: 0.058 ms, only the last of the three phases
choices.why: There are two stops per collection, at both ends of the mark, and the first one counts too.

prompt: A program prints the address of a heap value with `%p`, then again after a dozen collections, while still holding the pointer. What does the second line show?
hint: One word in `mgc.go` answers it.

choices.text: A different address, since collections pack live values together
choices.why: That would be a compacting collector, and `mgc.go` says Go's is non-compacting.

choices.text: The same address
choices.why: Right. The collector never moves a heap value; it reuses the gaps instead.

choices.text: `<nil>`, because the collector reset the pointer
choices.why: The collector never writes your variables. A value the program still points at is reachable and is kept, address and all.

choices.text: Something unpredictable, as the sweep may have reused that memory
choices.why: The sweep reuses only what marking did not reach, and this value was reached through the pointer.

prompt: Put the phases of one collection in order, as the runtime's documentation lists them.
hint: It begins and ends its marking with a short stop.
items: Mark and scan, alongside the program

prompt: A program keeps 8 MB alive and runs with `GOMEMLIMIT=4MiB`. What happens?
hint: The limit is soft.

choices.text: The runtime stops it with an out-of-memory error at 4 MiB
choices.why: Soft means no error at the limit: the program in section 04 finished.

choices.text: Allocations past 4 MiB return nil
choices.why: Go allocations do not return nil. The program kept allocating 496 MB in total.

choices.text: It finishes, slowly, collecting thousands of times
choices.why: Right: 2,927 collections and four times the run time, because no collection can free a reachable byte.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the heap is below 4 MiB anyway
choices.why: 8 MB alive is above 4 MiB; the collection count went from 61 to 2,927.

prompt: What does `GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=64MiB` ask of the runtime?
hint: The program of section 03 ran 10 collections under it.

choices.text: Never to collect, and to stop the program at 64 MiB
choices.why: It collected 10 times, and nothing stopped. A memory limit is respected even with `GOGC=off`.

choices.text: Not to collect until the memory it manages nears 64 MiB
choices.why: Right: 10 collections instead of 61, and a heap that grew to 63 MB and stopped there.

choices.text: To collect after every 64 MiB the program allocates
choices.why: The limit is about memory held, not memory allocated: a collection starts when what the runtime manages nears 64 MiB.

choices.text: Nothing: `GOGC=off` switches the memory limit off as well
choices.why: The two are separate settings, and the run under both collected 10 times rather than 0.

prompt: After `header = load()[:16]` and a full collection, `HeapAlloc` still counted 64 MB. Why?
hint: What does `header` point into?

choices.text: The collector had not run yet
choices.why: `heapMB` calls `runtime.GC` before measuring, so a whole collection had just finished.

choices.text: Slicing copied the 64 MB array
choices.why: Slicing copies nothing; that is why the slice could keep the original alive.

choices.text: `header` points into the 64 MB array, and the collector keeps all of it
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the collector looks at how much of an array a slice can see.

choices.text: `HeapAlloc` counts memory already freed as well
choices.why: After `strings.Clone` the same counter fell to 0 MB, so it does drop when memory is freed.

prompt: To keep a short substring without keeping the large string it came from, copy it with `strings.___`.
hint: `slices` has a function of the same name.

prompt: A service keeps about 300 MB alive and runs in a container limited to 512 MiB, with the default `GOGC`. What is the problem, and what fixes it?
hint: Work out the next goal under `GOGC=100`.

choices.text: The goal is about 600 MB, past the container; set `GOMEMLIMIT` a margin below 512 MiB
choices.why: Right. The proportion knows nothing of the container, and the limit makes the runtime collect before it gets there.

choices.text: None: the runtime reads the container's limit and stays under it
choices.why: The default memory limit is `math.MaxInt64`, which the documentation says effectively disables it.

choices.text: Collections are too frequent; set `GOGC=off` and nothing else
choices.why: With no limit beside it, `GOGC=off` collected nothing and grew to 499 MB for 8 MB alive.

choices.text: The heap is too big; set `GOMEMLIMIT=256MiB` to halve it
choices.why: That is under the 300 MB alive, the case where the lab program ran 2,927 collections and four times slower.

prompt: Which of these keep memory alive longer than the program needs it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask what a long-lived variable points into.

choices.text: A cache that stores `body[:20]` of each 1 MB request body for a day
choices.why: Yes. Each entry keeps its whole megabyte reachable.

choices.text: A map that stores `strings.Clone(line[:8])` for each line of a large file
choices.why: No: each key has eight bytes of its own, and the lines become unreachable.

choices.text: A package-level slice of pointers to finished jobs that nothing ever removes
choices.why: Yes. A package variable is a root, so every job it points at stays reachable for good.

choices.text: A 1 MB buffer inside a function that returns only its length
choices.why: No. Nothing leads to it after the return, so the next collection frees it, if it was on the heap at all.

prompt: You want to know whether a particular function's result is allocated on the heap. Which command answers that?
hint: The answer is decided before the program runs.

choices.text: `GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./prog`
choices.why: It reports collections and heap totals, not which value was put where.

choices.text: `go build -gcflags=-m`
choices.why: Right. The compiler prints its verdict per value, with the file and line.

choices.text: `go vet`, which reports allocations as suspicious
choices.why: Allocating is not a mistake, and `go vet` looks for mistakes.

choices.text: Reading `HeapAlloc` from `runtime.ReadMemStats` in the program
choices.why: That is one total for the whole heap; it cannot say which function's value is in it.

prompt: A function stores `&v`, the address of its local variable `v`, in a package-level map and returns. What does the compiler do with `v`?
hint: A package variable outlives every call.

choices.text: Keeps it in the frame, as `v` is not returned
choices.why: Returning is one way to escape, not the only one. Anything that can reach `v` after the call counts.

choices.text: Refuses to compile the store
choices.why: Storing the address of a local is legal Go; the compiler moves the value instead of refusing.

choices.text: Copies `v` into the map's own storage, so that the pointer is never needed
choices.why: The map holds a pointer, and a pointer has to point at the one `v`, not at a copy.

choices.text: Moves it to the heap, since the map still points at it after the return
choices.why: Right. `-m` would print `moved to heap: v`, as it did for `p` in `newPoint`.
